verses.text: But Saul, still breathing threats and slaughter against the disciples of the Lord, went to the high priest,
and asked for letters from him to the synagogues of Damascus, that if he found any who were of the Way, whether men or women, he might bring them bound to Jerusalem.
As he traveled, he got close to Damascus, and suddenly a light from the sky shone around him.
He fell on the earth, and heard a voice saying to him, “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?”
He said, “Who are you, Lord?” The Lord said, “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting.
But  rise up, and enter into the city, and you will be told what you must do.”
The men who traveled with him stood speechless, hearing the sound, but seeing no one.
Saul arose from the ground, and when his eyes were opened, he saw no one. They led him by the hand, and brought him into Damascus.
He was without sight for three days, and neither ate nor drank.
Now there was a certain disciple at Damascus named Ananias. The Lord said to him in a vision, “Ananias!” He said, “Behold, it’s me, Lord.”
The Lord said to him, “Arise, and go to the street which is called Straight, and inquire in the house of Judah  for one named Saul, a man of Tarsus. For behold, he is praying,
and in a vision he has seen a man named Ananias coming in, and laying his hands on him, that he might receive his sight.”
But Ananias answered, “Lord, I have heard from many about this man, how much evil he did to your saints at Jerusalem.
Here he has authority from the chief priests to bind all who call on your name.”
But the Lord said to him, “Go your way, for he is my chosen vessel to bear my name before the nations and kings, and the children of Israel.
For I will show him how many things he must suffer for my name’s sake.”

Ananias departed, and entered into the house. Laying his hands on him, he said, “Brother Saul, the Lord, who appeared to you on the road by which you came, has sent me, that you may receive your sight, and be filled with the Holy Spirit.”
Immediately something like scales fell from his eyes, and he received his sight. He arose and was baptized.
He took food and was strengthened. Saul stayed several days with the disciples who were at Damascus.
Immediately in the synagogues he proclaimed the Christ, that he is the Son of God.
All who heard him were amazed, and said, “Isn’t this he who in Jerusalem made havoc of those who called on this name? And he had come here intending to bring them bound before the chief priests!”
But Saul increased more in strength, and confounded the Jews who lived at Damascus, proving that this is the Christ.
When many days were fulfilled, the Jews conspired together to kill him,
but their plot became known to Saul. They watched the gates both day and night that they might kill him,
but his disciples took him by night, and let him down through the wall, lowering him in a basket.
When Saul had come to Jerusalem, he tried to join himself to the disciples; but they were all afraid of him, not believing that he was a disciple.

But Barnabas took him, and brought him to the apostles, and declared to them how he had seen the Lord on the way, and that he had spoken to him, and how at Damascus he had preached boldly in the name of Jesus.
He was with them entering into  Jerusalem,
preaching boldly in the name of the Lord Jesus.  He spoke and disputed against the Hellenists,  but they were seeking to kill him.
When the brothers  knew it, they brought him down to Caesarea, and sent him off to Tarsus.
So the assemblies throughout all Judea and Galilee and Samaria had peace, and were built up. They were multiplied, walking in the fear of the Lord and in the comfort of the Holy Spirit.
As Peter went throughout all those parts, he came down also to the saints who lived at Lydda.
There he found a certain man named Aeneas, who had been bedridden for eight years, because he was paralyzed.
Peter said to him, “Aeneas, Jesus Christ heals you. Get up and make your bed!” Immediately he arose.
All who lived at Lydda and in Sharon saw him, and they turned to the Lord.
Now there was at Joppa a certain disciple named Tabitha, which when translated, means Dorcas.  This woman was full of good works and acts of mercy which she did.
In those days, she became sick, and died. When they had washed her, they laid her in an upper room.
As Lydda was near Joppa, the disciples, hearing that Peter was there, sent two men  to him, imploring him not to delay in coming to them.

Peter got up and went with them. When he had come, they brought him into the upper room. All the widows stood by him weeping, and showing the coats and garments which Dorcas had made while she was with them.
Peter sent them all out, and knelt down and prayed. Turning to the body, he said, “Tabitha, get up!” She opened her eyes, and when she saw Peter, she sat up.
He gave her his hand, and raised her up. Calling the saints and widows, he presented her alive.
And it became known throughout all Joppa, and many believed in the Lord.
He stayed many days in Joppa with a tanner named Simon.

footnotes.content: Saul breathing out threats—what a picture of a man locked hard against the truth, running on fury and certainty. And yet the Lord sees him. Even zealotry in the wrong direction is still motion toward the One who can stop and turn it round.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He wanted letters, authority, power to bind. But the Lord who makes the universe never needs a signature to carry out His will. Saul's papers were just clay—Jesus was already walking the Damascus road.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The light on the Damascus road—a place old and famous for merchants, caravans, the long mile south from Syria. There, at the threshold of a city, the Lord met him with sudden grace, brighter than noon. Sometimes we meet Jesus at the edges, just as we're about to cross a line.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Saul, Saul"—the name repeated twice. Tenderness in the double call, even as judgment fell. Jesus knew him by name and knew his heart before the light ever touched his eyes.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Who are you, Lord?" The first honest question Saul asks. And the answer: "I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting." In one sentence, everything turned over—he was not fighting saints, he was fighting the risen Christ himself.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Rise up. Enter the city. Wait. Instructions so simple, so clear—no long sermon, no theology. The Lord speaks to a broken man in mercy: move into what comes next, and I will show you.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The men who came with Saul heard sound but saw no one. They stood speechless, watching their companion fall blind before an invisible voice. There is loneliness in that—to see the Lord's hand move while those beside you remain locked out.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Led by the hand into Damascus—from hunter to the hunted, from prosecutor to prisoner of grace. He rose up blind, stripped of all he'd leaned on, and was led like a child. That is how the Lord unmakes a man so He can remake him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Three days without food or drink, without light. Fasting that was not chosen but endured, a waiting in darkness and hunger. The Lord leaves room for His own to be terrified, to feel the weight of what's broken before the healing starts.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ananias—a disciple whose name means "the Lord is gracious." How fitting: the grace-bearer called by name in a vision, "Behold, it's me, Lord"—ready, willing, awake to the voice. We pray for such readiness in ourselves.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Straight Street in Damascus—a real street, running east and west through the old city. Even amid vision and miracle, the Lord speaks in concrete particulars: the place, the street name, the house. He is not lost in abstraction when He works.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Saul also praying, receiving a vision of Ananias before they meet. The Lord at work in the heart of the hunted man even before comfort comes—praying in the dark, searching, hungry for truth. Prayer met prayer at the threshold.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ananias speaks the fear aloud: "I have heard... how much evil." He does not hide his hesitation from the Lord, and the Lord does not scold him for it. Our doubts, spoken honestly to Jesus, become the place where He teaches us to trust.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The very ones Saul bound, the very name he wished to erase—and yet the Lord's intention is to use this man to speak that name before kings and nations. The Lord does not waste our former strength; He redirects it toward His purpose.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "A chosen vessel to bear my name." Not reformed, not rehabilitated—chosen, called from before this road, before his fury. The Lord does not pluck up a weed and use it because He has no other garden; He chooses the very one He wishes to transform.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "I will show him how many things he must suffer for my name's sake." The Lord speaks plainly: suffering lies ahead. Yet He does not say this to discourage Saul but to prepare him, to show that the grace of being chosen includes the cross of being faithful.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ananias called him "Brother Saul"—already, before sight returned, before baptism, the family bond was spoken. The disciples claimed him as their own. In that word, Saul knew he was forgiven, known, loved by those he had hunted.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Something like scales fell from his eyes—literal or metaphor, the scripture does not say. But what an image: the veil, the blindness, the hardness lifted in an instant. He saw, he rose, he was baptized. One moment, three salvations.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He took food and was strengthened. Such a simple thing—to feed the famished, to restore the body. The Lord does not ask us to stay broken longer than needful. Saul ate, and his flesh received what grace had begun in his soul.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Immediately in the synagogues—not waiting, not hiding, not nursing the newness of his faith in secret. Saul proclaimed Christ the Son of God in the very places where he had once hunted believers. The converted hunter becomes the proclaimed word.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Isn't this he who made havoc?" The witnesses could not hide their amazement—the man they feared was now declaring the One they feared. Transformation so radical that people struggle to believe it. Yet there he stood, and the testimony was true.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Saul increased in strength, confounded the Jews by proving Christ—the power that once hunted now argued, the certainty that once condemned now defended. The Lord took the very capacities Saul had bent toward darkness and turned them toward light.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When many days were fulfilled, they conspired to kill him. The hunters became the hunted. Saul had known what it was to hunt; now he would know what it was to be hunted. The cross he had been told to carry began its weight.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They watched the gates day and night—not a casual threat but siege, deliberate, relentless. And yet the Lord, who had already turned one man's heart from murder to faith, was watching too, and His hand proved stronger.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Lowered in a basket through the wall—the persecutor who once came with authority and letters now fled in darkness, dependent on the hands of brothers he had come to destroy. Grace strips us of dignity so we might keep our lives and our Lord.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When he came to Jerusalem, they were all afraid. They had seen him hunt before; how could they know the road had changed him? Fear born from memory is the last wound to heal, even after the Lord has moved the mountain.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Barnabas took him—the name means "son of encouragement," and he lived it. In the moment when the disciples' fear would have cast Saul out, one man spoke for him, told the truth, and opened the door. The church remembers those who stand for the doubted.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He was with them entering into Jerusalem—no longer an outsider, no longer a threat, but part of the body, walking in with the apostles. Belonging restored, not erased but genuinely healed, the prodigal not sent back to the fields but seated at the table.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He spoke and disputed against the Hellenists—the same boldness that hunted believers now defended them. But boldness in the wrong cause is ruinous; boldness in Christ's cause brings the cross. The Hellenists sought to kill him, and his persecution continued.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The brothers brought him down to Caesarea and sent him to Tarsus—his own city, his own home, far from the scene of his new faith's danger. Sometimes the Lord calls us to rest, to be sent away, to wait in quiet for the next chapter to write itself.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The assemblies throughout all Judea and Galilee and Samaria had peace, and were multiplied—the very regions Saul had once set out to bring to heel were now at peace because he had been turned. His conversion was not a private mercy; it reverberated through the whole church.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: As Peter went throughout all those parts, he came down also to the saints who lived at Lydda. The apostles kept moving, kept visiting, kept tending the flock. Ministry was not a sermon from a pulpit but a presence among the scattered, the suffering, the hidden.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Aeneas had been bedridden for eight years, paralyzed—a long imprisonment, his own body his cell. Eight years is long enough to forget what it felt like to stand. The Lord comes to those who have waited longest.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Jesus Christ heals you. Get up and make your bed!"—not a private transaction but a command given with such confidence, such direct simplicity. Peter speaks and then bids him to use the healing, to prove it by making the bed. Faith and action joined.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: All who lived at Lydda and in Sharon saw him—two regions of plain near the coast, once centers of commerce and life. The news of Aeneas's healing spread through the land like the word spread through synagogues, visible proof that the Lord was still moving, still touching, still alive.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Tabitha, which means Dorcas—her name given in both Aramaic and Greek, as if the scripture wanted all people to know her. She was full of good works and acts of mercy. What a monument: not that she was powerful or eloquent, but that she made garments and loved widows.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: She became sick and died. No long illness described, no lesson drawn from the sickness—only the fact of her death and the care taken to lay her out. Sometimes the scripture mourns without explaining. That too is enough.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Lydda was near Joppa, so the disciples sent for Peter, imploring him not to delay. Their urgency speaks of their love—they did not send casually; they sent in haste, as if the time between death and resurrection might be short. Sometimes faith looks like not waiting.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The widows stood weeping, showing the coats and garments which Dorcas had made. In their hands, the evidence of her love. The Lord does not call us to be great; He calls us to be faithful, and the faithful are seen in the lives they touched and the need they answered.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Peter sent them all out and knelt down and prayed—a moment alone with the Lord and the body. Prayer before the miracle, never the other way. The apostle did not assume his power; he bent his knee and asked, and then he spoke, and she woke.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He gave her his hand and raised her up, and presented her alive to the saints and widows. From death, restored to her people. Peter did not take glory for himself; he gave her back to those she loved, alive and whole.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: It became known throughout all Joppa, and many believed in the Lord—the resurrection of Dorcas preached with no sermon needed, only the fact that she walked and lived again. The Lord's works carry their own word.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He stayed many days in Joppa with a tanner named Simon. Readers today hear an echo in the ordinary—a man staying in a tradesman's house, eating common food, resting after miracles, as if the apostle's holiness did not require distance but company. We still learn by sitting with the faithful.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
